2. Facts giving rise to this appeal are that the predecessor of the appellant as the pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.8 of 1985 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Balaganj, Sylhet for preemption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act, 1950) stating, inter alia, that he was a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding. Opposite party Nos.2 and 3 (in the miscellaneous case) transferred the case land to the pre-emptee by three registered kabalas dated 17.10.1978, 22.03.1979 and 26.01.1980 without serving any notice upon the preemptor. The pre-emptee was a stranger in the case holding. The preemptor came to know about the said transfers in the month of Poush, 1391 B.S. when the pre-emptee disclosed to the pre-emptor that he had purchased the case land from opposite party Nos. 2 and 3. The pre-emptor then obtained the certified copies of the said kabalas on 15.01.1985 and 16.01.1985 respectively and got definite knowledge about the aforesaid transfers in question and then filed the preemption application on 22.01.1985. 

 7. From the order and the judgment respectively of the Courts below, it appears that both the Courts below concurrently found that there was no defect of party. Both the Courts below found that the preemption application was filed with in the statutory period of 4(four) months from the date of knowledge of the kabalas under preemption. The High Court Division concurred with the Courts below that the preemptor was a co-sharer by purchase   in the case holding, preemption proceedings did not suffer from "partial pre-emption" and that the preemption application was not bad for defect of party, but it reversed the decision of the Courts below on the point of limitation only. From the judgment of the High Court Division, it appears that in deciding the question of limitation, it found that in the preemption application, the preemptor stated that he came to know about the transfers in question in the middle of Poush 1391 B.S. when pre-emptee (opposite party No.1 in the miscellaneous case) disclosed to him that he purchased the case land along with other lands from opposite party Nos,2 and 3 (in the miscellaneous case) whereas, the preemptor in his deposition stated that the previous owners used to possess the case land through bargadar and in the month of Poush, 1391 B.S., he for the first time came to know from opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 that opposite party No.1 purchased the case land rom them. The High Court Division observed that PW1 "contradicted himself with respect to his statement as made in the application and as disposed in the case." The High Court Division further Observed that according to the application, 1 the preemptor came to know about the transfers in question from opposite party No, 1 whereas, in his cross-examination, he stated that he learnt about the transfers from opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 3, he did not disclose any other source of his knowledge in the application for preemption about the transfers in question excepting   that opposite party No.1 informed him. The High Court Division further observed that in the deposition of PW 1, he disclosed the source of two more persons, i.e. opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 though their names were not disclosed in the preemption application and further these two opposite parties, i.e. 2 and 3-4 were not examined by the preemptor to prove the case of the knowledge. Then the High Court Division re-assessed the evidence of the PWs and the OPWs and observed that the Courts below misread the evidence as well as failed to consider the material evidence and thus both the Courts below fell into an error in allowing the preemption application. 

 8. Let us see whether the High Court Division was correct in making the above observation and in giving the above finding about the knowledge of the preemptor in respect of the kabalas in question and then holding that the preemption application was barred by limitation. Statements about the knowledge of the kabalas under preemption have been made in paragraphs 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the preemption application which read as follows: 

 9. In the deposition, the preemptor specifically stated to the effect that the case land belonged to Madaris Ali who died leaving behind Moina Miah and Kacha Bibi as his heirs and used to possess the case land through bargadar, Subahan and others used to barga cultivate the case land and he for the first part in the month of Poush, 1391 B.S. came to know about the transfers in question from opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 3. He further asserted that he did not know about the transfers in question and that the case land was sold secretly and the kabalas were also executed secretly and on coming to know about the sales in question, he obtained the certified copies of the kabalas and then came to know that opposite party No.1 purchased the case land by three kabalas dated 22.03.1997, 26.01.1980 and 17.10.1978. The relevant portion of the deposition of PW1 is quoted below verbatim: 

 10. From the statements made in the application for preemption as quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that the preemptor specifically stated that he came to know about the transfers in question from opposite party No.1, i.e. the pre-emptee when he disclosed that he purchased the case land from opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 in the month of Poush, 1391 B.S. and the pre-emptor as PW1 asserted the same fact in his examination-in-chief. Therefore, we find no contradiction between the facts stated in the application for preemption and the deposition of PW1. The High Court Division failed to consider a very pertinent fact of the case that although PW 1 categorically asserted about his knowledge of the transfers in question in the month of Poush, 1391 B.S., but during cross-examination, the pre-emptee did not at all challenge the said assertion made by PW1 in his examination-in-chief. It may further be stated that PW1 in his cross-examination re-asserted the said fact. PW1 in his cross-examination also asserted the fact that the pre-emptee used to barga cultivate the land of opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 along with other lands for 10/12 years and before that the other people named Abdul Mannaf used to barga cultivate the case land. Besides the above, PW3 also asserted the fact that Abdus Subhan, opposite party No.1, i.e. the pre-emptee used to barga cultivate the case land. In cross-examination, he also asserted   that opposite party No.1 used to barga cultivate the land of opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 including the case land. OPW 1, the son of the pre-emptee who was substituted as preemptee No. 1 (Ka) in his examination-in-chief, did not at all deny the fact of knowledge as asserted by the preemptor, but unfortunately, the High Court Division failed to consider the above mentioned material evidence of the PWs and the OPWs.
